description: Step 2 of the lint, and the one that returns findings. Pass the activities and jurisdictions set_profile validated, and get lint-style findings: which obligations apply, with severity (warn/info), citation, as_of_date, staleness, and confidence. warn: a live obligation binds the profile (obligation), a posture finding needs attention (posture), or LexLint lacks current data for a declared jurisdiction (coverage). info: context rather than a live duty, and kind says which it is: an instrument LexLint cannot say is in force today (pending), a jurisdiction-wide statement of how the local law treats crawling as a whole, binding nobody on its own (posture), a note about what was not reported (coverage), a duty your customer, a public body or a financial institution, owes and meets through your software (customer_duty, with public_sector or regulated_sector declared; triage it in the product lane), an instrument whose owed is not yours (obligation), or, with derived: true, a record an app holds to meet the deadlines the matched laws set, LexLint's inference traced to each law (derived; triage it in the code lane). LexLint never reports error: a lint cannot be sure something is prohibited, so it will not say so. Every instrument finding also carries certainty.resultset, which is the axis to present on and is NOT the same cut as kind: present is law as it stands today, including an instrument blocked by a court, whose enforcement is paused (a live risk held in abeyance, never hypothetical); forward is law that may be coming; historical is a spent instrument that is neither. NOTHING IN forward MAY GATE: it is informational, it must never reach an exit code, fail a build, or block a merge, and a bill in committee changing your build colour is a misuse of this tool. Within forward, certainty.rung orders by how much is PINNED to primary text and never by a probability, with rung 1 (enacted, commencement dated) predicting nothing at all; certainty.rung is null where the law library holds no stage to rank by, which is not the same as the lowest rung. If you suppress any part of forward from what you show a user, say so in your output: a run that drops rows and then reports "no basic issues found" is a silent pass. Each instrument finding also carries in_force, whose `words` is what to print wherever you say when a law binds. Obligations are matched from AI, scraping, privacy, cybersecurity, communications, content-moderation, product-liability, digital-accessibility, digital-identity, cloud-service, export-control, age-gating and reuse law; that is every topic the law library carries, so a declaration can raise findings from any of them and no topic is served by get_law alone any more. A finding whose instrument has a LexLint page carries note_url; show the citation as a link to it, and never construct that URL yourself. A jurisdiction LexLint has no current data for is a WARNING, never a silent pass, and the passing state is "no basic issues found", never "compliant". This is a lint for catching basic issues early, NOT legal advice and NOT a compliance certification. Costs three upstream requests for any number of declared jurisdictions: it reads the whole published law library and filters to your declaration in memory, rather than one request per jurisdiction. A trial key lints at most 10 distinct jurisdictions over its whole life; a declaration past that is refused before anything is spent. A repeat lint against a law library that has not moved since an earlier one can cost fewer, served from this key's own cache. This tool needs sign-in or an UnGovr Open Data key (metered per request; get one at https://ungovr.org/cli-login?client=lexlint).

activities.description: What the app does, from the profile set_profile returned. Allowed: crawls_web, trains_models, generates_content, deploys_chatbot, deploys_companion_chatbot, deploys_mental_health_chatbot, automated_outreach, high_risk_decisions, processes_voice, processes_biometrics, processes_personal_data, publishes_adult_content, operates_social_platform, serves_minors, operates_app_store, ships_mobile_app, ships_consumer_interface, relies_on_digital_identity, collects_e_signatures, ships_encryption, serves_sanctioned_destination, aggregates_content, distributes_software_product, handles_health_records, provides_financial_services, operates_essential_service, is_listed_company, provides_telecom_services, provides_cloud_services, statutory_requests, records_calls, records_text_chat, tracks_devices, is_bank, is_lender, is_insurer, is_securities_firm, is_payment_provider, is_crypto_asset_provider, employment_decisions, credit_decisions, insurance_decisions, housing_decisions, education_decisions, health_care_decisions, public_services_decisions, justice_decisions, generates_text, generates_images, generates_video, generates_audio

activities_left_out.description: Activities the developer was asked about and said this software does not do. Today it answers processes_personal_data: unsent, a declaration naming any activity its code settles is matched as if it processes personal data, with an info coverage line, until the developer answers. It also answers the two chatbot kinds: deploys_chatbot with neither declared nor left out is matched as if it is both, with an info coverage line. From the profile set_profile returned.

brief.description: Send true when you will show these findings to a person and have no LexLint procedure loaded. Each finding then comes back as one line to print: its summary and first duty clipped to 160 characters, with the citation, note_url, in_force, owed and kind; the full text of any law is one get_law call away. Leave it out when you write lexlint.yml: brief findings drop fields the manifest keeps.

client_version.description: The LexLint plugin version you are running, from your SKILL.md, exactly as check_access takes it. Send it on every lint: a run that skips the preflight otherwise learns nothing about its own staleness. Omitted, update_available comes back null, which means LexLint learned nothing, never that you are current.

derived.description: true adds derived findings: the records an app holds to meet the deadlines the matched laws set, inferred by LexLint and traced to each law. false leaves them out; omitted, the server default applies.

flows.description: Where this software stores or sends personal data across a border, one entry per route: [{"from": "eu", "to": "us", "data": "personal", "basis": "contract_clauses"}]. from and to are jurisdiction slugs, as jurisdictions takes them; data is personal or sensitive; basis is the transfer mechanism the route relies on: adequacy, contract_clauses, binding_rules, certification, authority_approval, consent, derogation, unknown. [] when asked and no personal data leaves the jurisdiction it was collected in. Ask the developer; never infer it from the code. Each cross-border transfer finding then names the declared flows that leave its jurisdiction. No finding is dropped or downgraded on a flow.

jurisdictions.description: Jurisdiction slugs from the profile set_profile returned, lowercase, "/"-separated (e.g. "us", "us/ca", "eu", "kr"). A slug is the jurisdiction's UnGovr Atlas path: California is https://ungovr.org/us/ca and its Atlas ID is urn:ungovr:us/ca. Its ISO 3166 code, US-CA, is accepted too. A deeper or unresearched path resolves to the nearest jurisdiction with law, and the jurisdictions whose law is researched are listed at https://lexlint.io/law for the developer to check; name every jurisdiction the app operates in: one left off is unlinted, not passed.

public_sector.description: Is this software run by a public body (body), sold to or run for public bodies (supplier), both, or neither (none)? Ask the developer every time the profile is declared; never infer it from the code. Omitted, duties binding only public bodies are reported as the caller's, and run_lint counts them in a coverage line.

public_sector_functions.description: Which kinds of public body run or buy this software. Ask only when public_sector is body or supplier, and never infer it from the code. One or more of: general (a general-purpose public body, such as a city hall, a state department or a federal agency), law_enforcement (police and sheriffs), corrections (prisons, jails, parole and probation), prosecution_courts (courts, prosecutors and public defenders), public_education (public schools, school districts and public universities), public_health (health departments and public hospitals), elections (election offices), public_benefits (agencies deciding welfare, unemployment or Medicaid eligibility), emergency_services (911 centers, fire and emergency medical services). A duty that binds only another kind is reported as someone else's; a duty that binds every public body always reaches you. Omitted, every public-body duty reaches you, and run_lint counts the ones that bind a single kind in a coverage line.

regulated_sector.description: Whose duty a financial-law row is. Is this software run by a bank, insurer or other regulated financial entity (body), supplied to one (supplier), or neither (none)? {"financial": "supplier"}. Ask when provides_financial_services or a license class (is_bank, is_lender, is_insurer, is_securities_firm, is_payment_provider, is_crypto_asset_provider) is declared; never infer it. It routes and never matches, so a supplier still declares the classes of its customers. Omitted, the entity's duties are reported as the caller's, and run_lint counts them in a coverage line.

roles.description: Which role this software's maker holds under each regime, keyed by axis: ai_system (provider, deployer, importer, distributor, product_manufacturer, authorised_representative, the EU AI Act's operators) and personal_data (controller, processor, the GDPR's). {"ai_system": ["provider"], "personal_data": ["processor"]}; "none" alone when asked and none applies. Ask the developer; never infer it from the code. Omitted, an axis routes nothing and run_lint counts the duties a role would move in a coverage line.

title: Lint an app against the law
